title: Mean, median, mode and range
blurb: Calculate mean, median, mode and range without the classic slips, find a missing value from a mean, and weight a mean correctly.
question: Aaliyah needs a mean of 80 across five prerequisite quizzes. Her first four scores are 76, 84, 71 and 83. What must she score on the fifth quiz, and how would her median and range change?

teach.body: Formally, measures of central tendency (mean, median and mode) summarize a data set with one typical value, and the range measures its spread. In plain English: the mean is the 'fair share' if everything were split evenly, the median is the middle value once the data are lined up, the mode is the most common value, and the range is the distance from the smallest value to the largest.

items.label: Mean: add every value, divide by how many
Mode: the most frequent value (none, one or several)

teach.h: Worked example: patients seen per hour (odd count)
items: Data for 7 hours at a walk-in clinic: 6, 9, 4, 9, 12, 5, 11.
Median: with 7 values the middle is the 4th: 9. Mode: 9 (it appears twice). Range: 12 − 4 = 8.

steps.label: Order the data
steps.sub: Smallest to largest. Never skip this.

teach.h: Worked example: resting heart rates (even count)
items: Order: 64, 68, 70, 72, 75, 77, 80, 90. The two middle values are the 4th and 5th: 72 and 75.
Median = (72 + 75) ÷ 2 = 73.5. It doesn't have to be one of the data values.

teach.h: The mode, and data that aren't numbers
teach.body: A data set can have no mode (nothing repeats), one mode, or two or more (bimodal when two values tie for most frequent). The mode is reported as the VALUE, not the number of times it appears. It is also the only one of the three that works for categorical data: you can find the most common blood type, but not the 'mean blood type.'

items: Aaliyah needs a mean of 80 over 5 quizzes. Total needed = mean × count = 80 × 5 = 400.
With 86 her scores order to 71, 76, 83, 84, 86: median 83, range 86 − 71 = 15.

head: Category
Weight
Score
Weight × score
teach.caption: When categories count differently, multiply each score by its weight and add. The plain average (78 + 90 + 95) ÷ 3 = 87.7 is wrong here.

teach.h: Mean, median and mode side by side

teach.text: Classic slips: taking the middle of the list as written instead of ordering it; picking one of the two middle values when n is even; reporting the mode as how many times it appears; range as last value minus first; and averaging group means when the groups are different sizes.

items: Mean = sum ÷ count. Missing value: total needed (mean × count) minus the known sum.
Median: order first; even count = average of the two middle values.
Mode: the most frequent value; there may be none or several.
Range = maximum − minimum, never last − first.
Weighted mean: multiply by the weights and add; combine groups by totals, not by averaging their means.

summary: You can now calculate the mean, median, mode and range of any data set, including even counts and repeated values, find a missing value from a target mean, and compute weighted and combined means. You also know the five classic slips that TEAS distractors are built on.

A.q: A nurse records the number of pain-free hours for 9 patients after surgery: 14, 9, 22, 11, 9, 17, 25, 12, 16. What is the median?
A.why: Order the data: 9, 9, 11, 12, 14, 16, 17, 22, 25. With 9 values the median is the 5th: 14.

whyNot.0: 9 is the 5th value in the list as written (and the mode). The data must be ordered first.
whyNot.1: 12 is the 4th ordered value; the middle of 9 values is the 5th.
whyNot.3: 15 is the mean (135 ÷ 9), not the median.

A.q: A pharmacy technician's mean number of prescriptions filled over 6 shifts is 48. The first 5 shifts were 45, 52, 39, 50 and 47. How many prescriptions were filled on the 6th shift?
A.why: Total = mean × count = 48 × 6 = 288. Known sum: 45 + 52 + 39 + 50 + 47 = 233. Sixth shift: 288 − 233 = 55. Check: 288 ÷ 6 = 48.

whyNot.0: 7 uses 48 × 5 = 240 as the total, multiplying by the wrong count.
whyNot.1: 47 is the median of the first five shifts, not the missing value.
whyNot.2: 48 assumes the missing shift equals the mean, which would only happen if the other five also averaged 48 (they average 46.6).

A.q: A blood drive records donors' blood types: O, A, O, B, A, AB, O, A, B, A, O. What is the mode of the data?
A.why: Count each type: O appears 4 times, A 4 times, B 2 times and AB once. O and A tie for most frequent, so the data are bimodal: A and O.

whyNot.0: Type O appears 4 times, but so does type A, so O alone is incomplete.
whyNot.2: Type A appears 4 times, but so does type O, so A alone is incomplete.
whyNot.3: Two types tie for most frequent; a tie gives two modes, not none.

B.q: Hemoglobin levels (g/dL) for 10 patients are 13.2, 11.8, 14.6, 12.4, 15.1, 12.9, 13.8, 11.5, 14.0 and 12.4. What is the median?

whyNot.0: 12.9 is the 5th value alone; with an even count, average the 5th and 6th.
whyNot.2: 13.17 is the mean (131.7 ÷ 10), not the median.
whyNot.3: 13.2 is the 6th value alone; with an even count, average the 5th and 6th.

B.q: A patient's daily step counts from Monday to Sunday are 8,200; 5,900; 11,400; 7,300; 4,800; 9,600; 6,100. What is the range?

whyNot.0: 2,100 is the difference between the first and last days listed (8,200 − 6,100), not the extremes.
whyNot.1: 4,100 is the maximum minus the median (11,400 − 7,300).
whyNot.2: 5,500 subtracts 5,900, the second-smallest value, instead of the minimum, 4,800.

B.q: In a prerequisite course, exams count 60%, labs 25% and quizzes 15%. Javier averages 74 on exams, 92 on labs and 88 on quizzes. What is his course grade? Round to the nearest tenth.

whyNot.1: 84.7 is the plain average (74 + 92 + 88) ÷ 3, which ignores the weights.
whyNot.2: 86.9 swaps the exam and lab weights: 0.60 × 92 + 0.25 × 74 + 0.15 × 88.
whyNot.3: 88 is the median of the three category scores.

C.q: The mean length of stay for 8 patients on a unit is 4.5 days. A 9th patient is discharged after 13.5 days. What is the new mean length of stay for all 9 patients?
C.why: Old total = 4.5 × 8 = 36 days. New total = 36 + 13.5 = 49.5. New mean = 49.5 ÷ 9 = 5.5.

whyNot.1: 6.0 adds 13.5 ÷ 9 = 1.5 to the old mean, which treats the old mean as if it were already a total over 9.
whyNot.2: 6.2 divides the new total, 49.5, by 8 instead of 9.
whyNot.3: 9.0 averages the old mean with the new value, (4.5 + 13.5) ÷ 2, as if each were one data point.

C.q: A thermometer was found to read 0.4 °F low, so 0.4 °F is added to every temperature in a patient data set. Which statement is correct?
options: Mean and range both rise by 0.4
Mean rises by 0.4; range is unchanged
Mean is unchanged; range rises by 0.4
Mean rises by 0.4; median is unchanged
C.why: Adding the same amount to every value shifts the mean, median and mode up by that amount, but the gap between the largest and smallest values stays the same, so the range is unchanged.

whyNot.0: Max and min both rise by 0.4, so their difference (the range) does not change.
whyNot.2: The mean moves with the data; the range is what stays the same.
whyNot.3: The median shifts by 0.4 too, just like the mean.

C.q: A morning class of 20 students averaged 76 on a dosage-calculation quiz, and an afternoon class of 30 students averaged 86. What is the mean score of all 50 students?

whyNot.1: 81 averages the two class means, which ignores that the afternoon class is larger.
whyNot.3: 86 is the afternoon mean. The larger class pulls the result toward 86, but the 20 morning scores still count.

reteach.title: Splitting the pizza bill
reteach.question: Five friends order food: $12, $9, $15, $9 and $30. How do 'split it evenly,' 'the middle order' and 'the most common order' match the mean, median and mode?

blocks.body: The total is $75. Split evenly, each pays $75 ÷ 5 = $15: that's the mean. Line the orders up ($9, $9, $12, $15, $30) and the middle one is $12: the median. Two people ordered $9 meals: the mode. The gap from the cheapest to the priciest order is $30 − $9 = $21: the range. Notice the $30 order drags the mean up to $15, while the median stays at $12.

blocks.caption: Mean $15 (fair share), median $12 (middle), mode $9 (most common), range $21.

blocks.text: The mode is the VALUE that repeats ($9), not how many times it repeats (2).

explain.body: Add every value and divide by how many values there are. To find a missing value, multiply the mean by the count to get the total, then subtract the values you know.

steps.label: Add all values
steps.sub: Recheck the sum a second way

steps.label: Divide by the count
steps.sub: Count the values, not the largest one

test.q: A patient's fluid intake over 4 days was 1,850 mL, 2,100 mL, 1,650 mL and 2,400 mL. What was the mean daily intake?

whyNot.0: 750 mL is the range (2,400 − 1,650), a measure of spread.
whyNot.3: 2,025 mL averages only the smallest and largest values.

explain.body: Order the data first. With an odd count, the median is the middle value. With an even count, it is the mean of the two middle values.

test.q: The ages of 6 patients in a waiting room are 34, 77, 52, 29, 66 and 48. What is the median age?
test.why: Ordered: 29, 34, 48, 52, 66, 77. With 6 values, average the 3rd and 4th: (48 + 52) ÷ 2 = 50.

whyNot.0: 40.5 averages the middle two values of the unordered list (52 and 29).
whyNot.1: 48 is the 3rd ordered value alone; average the 3rd and 4th.
whyNot.3: 51 is the mean (306 ÷ 6), not the median.

explain.body: The value that occurs most often. Report the value itself. If two values tie for most frequent, both are modes; if nothing repeats, there is no mode.

test.q: A clinic records the shoe sizes of 9 nursing students for a uniform order: 8, 9, 7, 9, 10, 8, 11, 9, 8. What is the mode?
test.why: Sizes 8 and 9 each appear 3 times, more than any other size, so the data are bimodal: 8 and 9.

whyNot.1: 9 appears 3 times, but 8 also appears 3 times, so both are modes.
whyNot.2: 3 is how many times each mode appears, not the mode itself.
whyNot.3: Values do repeat; a tie between two values gives two modes.

explain.body: Range = largest value − smallest value. Find the true maximum and minimum anywhere in the list; the first and last values written are not necessarily the extremes.

test.q: A patient's blood glucose readings, in mg/dL, are 142, 98, 175, 120, 88 and 131. What is the range?

whyNot.0: 11 is the difference between the first and last readings listed (142 − 131).
whyNot.1: 54 subtracts the minimum from the first reading (142 − 88) instead of from the maximum.
whyNot.2: 77 subtracts 98, the second-smallest reading, instead of the minimum, 88.
